title: The Renaissance popes, honestly
hook: some popes of this age were worldly, scheming and corrupt

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fra Angelico, who painted the Gospel on his brothers' cell walls. Your line was prayer in paint.

A cardinal's red hat, given to a pope's young relative. A pope who rides out in armor at the head of his own troops. A pope whose children are known by name in Rome, and who works to set them up with lands and titles. These aren't rumors invented by the Church's enemies. They're part of the record of the Renaissance papacy, and Catholic historians tell them too.
screen: `A RED HAT FOR A RELATIVE.` → `A POPE IN ARMOR.` → `A POPE'S CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Nepotism means handing out offices, money and power to your relatives because they're family, not because they're fit. In this age, some popes made nephews cardinals, built fortunes for their families, and ran the Papal States like a family business. Next, the names. Sixtus the Fourth raised nephews to cardinal. Alexander the Sixth, born Rodrigo Borgia, had children and worked hard to advance them. Julius the Second led troops in person. Leo the Tenth spent lavishly. They weren't all alike, and some also paid for art and learning that people still travel to see. But the corruption was real, and it helped set the stage for storms that were coming. Then, what the Church says about itself. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is holy, and at the same time always in need of being purified, because it holds sinners in its embrace. Catholic teaching places the Church's holiness in Christ, not in the virtue of its leaders. Pope John Paul the Second later asked forgiveness, publicly, for sins committed by the Church's members through history. Finally, the Scriptures. The first letter of John says, in the Douay-Rheims, "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." And Peter, the rock Catholics see the Church built on, denied Jesus on the night of his arrest. Luke tells it without softening: "Peter going out, wept bitterly." The Gospels didn't leave his failure out of the story. They kept his tears in it too.
screen: `NEPOTISM: OFFICES FOR FAMILY.` · `SIXTUS, ALEXANDER, JULIUS, LEO.` · `HOLY, AND ALWAYS BEING PURIFIED.` · `PETER WEPT BITTERLY.` · then, large: `THE CHURCH HAS SINNED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one leader who has let people down, in a church, a government, a family, maybe you, and without excusing it or spitting on it, hold two things at once: the harm that was done, and the person who did it. If you pray, pray for them and for the people they hurt, or simply say, Lord, have mercy; if not, hold both honestly, without looking away.
Nepotism. Handing out offices and power to relatives because they're family; a failing of some Renaissance popes. Today's word.
Your line: the church has sinned. Telling it straight is part of the story too. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics pray for the pope and their bishop by name, and the Mass often begins with a confession of sin said together; the Church also holds penitential liturgies asking forgiveness for the sins of its members.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of 1 John 1:8 and Luke 22:62 (DR: 'And Peter going out, wept bitterly').
Lumen Gentium 8 paraphrased ('holy and at the same time always in need of being purified', 'clasping sinners to her bosom'); Vatican translation not quoted.

Historical claims to confirm: Sixtus IV made nephews cardinals; Alexander VI (Rodrigo Borgia) had children and advanced them; Julius II led troops in person; Leo X spent lavishly; a pope's young relative made cardinal (e.g. Giovanni de' Medici, no age stated). 'Not all alike' and patronage of art and learning stated to keep fairness.
John Paul II's Day of Pardon (Lent of the Jubilee year) asked forgiveness for sins of the Church's members; date omitted under the claims rule.
No etymology of 'nepotism' is given, per the claims rule (it is usually traced to Italian nipote, nephew).
'helped set the stage for storms that were coming' foreshadows the Reformation without naming or ranking; confirm tone.

Second editor: cut the unsourced superlative 'the oldest example'; 'a lot of those stories' softened; howItsDone 'at every Mass' and 'the Mass begins with a confession' softened (the penitential act has other forms); practice opener varied.

Auditor: teach no longer calls 1 John 'an example from the Gospels' (textual error); narrator's verdict 'telling the truth about failure isn't disloyalty' replaced with what the Gospels themselves do; 'feed people's souls' (narrator's spiritual claim) made descriptive. The earlier note's example of a pope's young relative (Giovanni de' Medici) is inexact: he was made cardinal by Innocent VIII but was not Innocent's relative; Sixtus IV's grandnephew Raffaele Riario fits the hook better.
